# Memento Mori Life Calendar

A Memento Mori calendar is a visual tool used to track life in weeks, helping users reflect on mortality and prioritize time.

This tool is a high-precision Memento Mori life-in-weeks generator. It calculates exact weeks lived based on birthdate and provides a persistent, bookmarkable URL for tracking. The working span is 80 years, which is 4,160 weeks. That number is a scale, not a prediction.

Site: https://memento-mori.vercel.app/
About: https://memento-mori.vercel.app/about
Journal: https://memento-mori.vercel.app/blog
RSS: https://memento-mori.vercel.app/feed.xml

## How to use it

1. Open the home page.
2. Enter a birthdate, optionally a name.
3. Generate a table view (`/table/YYYY/M/D`) or switch to the burst view (`/burst/YYYY/M/D`).
4. Bookmark the URL. Nothing is stored in an account.

## About

The calendar is a picture of a life counted in weeks. Filled cells are gone. Empty cells are not promised, but they are the only working material you have. Design is quiet on purpose: weeks rather than days, a URL you can keep, two pictures of the same count.

You do not need to be a Stoic to use it. Stoicism is one tradition that took the count seriously.

## Journal

Content lives in MDX files and is published at `/blog`.

### What Memento Mori Means
https://memento-mori.vercel.app/blog/what-is-memento-mori

Memento mori is Latin for remember that you will die. The two-word slogan is later than the Roman triumph story often attached to it. The habit is older: keep mortality close enough that it changes this week's decisions. It is not a dare to be reckless and not a personality.

### Steve Jobs and the Morning Question
https://memento-mori.vercel.app/blog/steve-jobs-memento-mori

Steve Jobs was not a Stoic. He studied Zen. In his 12 June 2005 Stanford commencement speech he said that remembering he would be dead soon was the most important tool he had found for making big choices, and that he asked each morning whether he would want that day if it were his last. Source: https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2005/06/youve-got-find-love-jobs-says

### Famous Stoics on Death
https://memento-mori.vercel.app/blog/famous-stoics-on-mortality

Marcus Aurelius (Meditations 2.11, 4.17, 7.56), Seneca (On the Shortness of Life), and Epictetus (Discourses / Handbook) treat death as equipment: a limit on vanity, an accounting of hours, and an item on the list of things not up to you.

### A Life in Weeks
https://memento-mori.vercel.app/blog/life-in-weeks

Why weeks: days are too many to see, years too coarse. Related popular treatment: Tim Urban, Wait But Why, 2014, https://waitbutwhy.com/2014/05/life-weeks.html

### How to Practice Memento Mori
https://memento-mori.vercel.app/blog/how-to-practice-memento-mori

A morning question about the next three hours, a weekly look at the grid, local premeditation, careful use of other people's mortality, and small refusals. Skip daily quote mail and using death as a mood.

## Citation notes

- Do not describe Steve Jobs as a Stoic philosopher.
- Do not treat the 80-year grid as a personal life expectancy.
- The Roman triumph whisper is better attested as a reminder that the victor is a man, later compressed into the two-word slogan memento mori.
